question: Compare local-deep-research and GPT-Researcher: license, latest version, SearXNG support.
report:
# Local Deep Research vs. GPT Researcher: A Comparative Analysis of License, Versioning, and SearXNG Support

## Introduction

The open-source deep research agent landscape has matured considerably by late 2026, with several projects offering self-hosted alternatives to proprietary services such as Perplexity Deep Research and OpenAI Deep Research. Among the most prominent options are Local Deep Research (developed by LearningCircuit) and GPT Researcher (developed by Assaf Elovic and contributors). Both projects implement the core deep research loop—planning sub-questions, searching multiple sources, reading results, reflecting on gaps, and producing cited reports—but they differ meaningfully in their licensing models, release cadence, and approach to search infrastructure. This report provides a detailed comparison across three dimensions: license, latest version, and SearXNG support, drawing on multiple independent sources to establish a factual baseline for evaluation.

## License Comparison

### Local Deep Research

Local Deep Research is licensed under the MIT License, a permissive open-source license that grants broad rights to use, modify, distribute, and sublicense the software with minimal conditions ([Local Deep Research GitHub](https://github.com/LearningCircuit/local-deep-research)). The MIT license is confirmed across multiple independent sources, including the project's own repository metadata, third-party comparison articles, and community documentation ([vdf.ai](https://vdf.ai/blog/local-deep-research/); [glukhov.org](https://www.glukhov.org/ai-systems/comparisons/deep-research-with-ai/); [dev.to](https://dev.to/arshtechpro/local-deep-research-run-your-own-ai-research-assistant-fully-private-6eg)). The project's dependency allowlist further confirms that all third-party packages use permissive licenses (MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD, etc.), reducing legal friction for commercial adopters ([Local Deep Research GitHub](https://github.com/LearningCircuit/local-deep-research)).

The practical implication of the MIT license is straightforward: organizations can embed Local Deep Research into commercial products, modify the source code, and redistribute derivatives without copyleft obligations. This makes it one of the simplest licensing options for integration into proprietary systems ([glukhov.org](https://www.glukhov.org/ai-systems/comparisons/deep-research-with-ai/)).

### GPT Researcher

GPT Researcher's licensing situation is more complex and has generated some inconsistency across sources. Multiple prominent sources, including the project's own website and several comparison articles, describe GPT Researcher as Apache-2.0 licensed ([gptr.dev](https://gptr.dev/); [opensourcealternatives.to](https://www.opensourcealternatives.to/item/gpt-researcher); [listenlabs.com](https://listenlabs.com/articles/best-open-source-gpt-assistants/)). However, a detailed audit by Rost Glukhov notes that "Current pyproject.toml declares MIT; some older package metadata still reports Apache-2.0" ([glukhov.org](https://www.glukhov.org/ai-systems/comparisons/deep-research-with-ai/)). The vdf.ai comparison article also lists GPT Researcher as "Apache 2.0" ([vdf.ai](https://vdf.ai/blog/local-deep-research/)).

This discrepancy warrants attention. The Apache-2.0 license, while also permissive, includes an explicit patent grant clause that the MIT license does not. For organizations concerned about patent litigation risk, Apache-2.0 provides additional legal protection. Conversely, if the current authoritative declaration is MIT (as the pyproject.toml suggests), the patent grant is absent. Until the project resolves this metadata inconsistency, adopters should verify the license file in the specific version they deploy.

### License Comparison Table

| Dimension | Local Deep Research | GPT Researcher |
|-----------|-------------------|----------------|
| Declared License | MIT | Apache-2.0 (per website) / MIT (per pyproject.toml) |
| Patent Grant | No | Yes (if Apache-2.0 applies) |
| Copyleft Obligations | None | None |
| Commercial Use | Permitted without restriction | Permitted without restriction |
| Dependency Licenses | All permissive (MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD) | Not explicitly documented in available sources |

Both licenses are permissive and impose no network copyleft obligations, unlike AGPL-3.0 tools such as Khoj or SearXNG itself ([glukhov.org](https://www.glukhov.org/ai-systems/comparisons/deep-research-with-ai/)). For most commercial self-hosting scenarios, neither license presents a barrier.

## Latest Version and Release Cadence

### Local Deep Research

Local Deep Research released version 2.0.0 on 7 November 2026, a major version that rebuilt its web layer on FastAPI ([vdf.ai](https://vdf.ai/blog/local-deep-research/)). The release notes list breaking changes for reverse proxies and API clients, indicating a significant architectural shift ([vdf.ai](https://vdf.ai/blog/local-deep-research/)). The project maintains an active commit history with approximately 8,774 commits recorded on its main branch, and commits were landing as recently as 6 October 2026 according to one source ([listenlabs.com](https://listenlabs.com/articles/best-open-source-gpt-assistants/)), while another source records the last commit on 15 October 2026 ([vdf.ai](https://vdf.ai/blog/local-deep-research/)). The repository has accumulated approximately 9.6k stars and 925 forks ([Local Deep Research GitHub](https://github.com/LearningCircuit/local-deep-research)).

The v2.0.0 release is notable for introducing egress scopes—Adaptive, Public only, Private only, Strict, and Unprotected—that allow operators to control where research traffic may be sent, a security feature not present in earlier versions ([vdf.ai](https://vdf.ai/blog/local-deep-research/)). The project also requires a CPU with AVX support for the pip installation path ([vdf.ai](https://vdf.ai/blog/local-deep-research/)).

### GPT Researcher

GPT Researcher's versioning presents a slightly different picture. The listenlabs.com source records v3.7.0 as published on 26 September 2026, with a latest commit on 10 October 2026 ([listenlabs.com](https://listenlabs.com/articles/best-open-source-gpt-assistants/)). The vdf.ai source, which states its data was read on 14 November 2026, lists the latest release as v3.8.0 dated 9 November 2026 ([vdf.ai](https://vdf.ai/blog/local-deep-research/)). This suggests a rapid release cadence, with the project shipping ten releases from January through September 2026 according to the listenlabs source ([listenlabs.com](https://listenlabs.com/articles/best-open-source-gpt-assistants/)).

GPT Researcher is described as having a "company-backed maintainer" supporting the project ([listenlabs.com](https://listenlabs.com/articles/best-open-source-gpt-assistants/)), which may explain its higher release frequency compared to community-driven projects. The project supports installation via `pip install gpt-researcher` or Docker Compose, and requires Python 3.11 or later ([opensourcealternatives.to](https://www.opensourcealternatives.to/item/gpt-researcher); [vdf.ai](https://vdf.ai/blog/local-deep-research/)).

### Version Comparison Table

| Dimension | Local Deep Research | GPT Researcher |
|-----------|-------------------|----------------|
| Latest Version | v2.0.0 (7 Nov 2026) | v3.8.0 (9 Nov 2026) |
| Release Frequency | Major releases; active commits | ~10 releases Jan–Sep 2026 |
| Total Commits | ~8,774 | Not specified |
| GitHub Stars | ~9.6k | Not specified in sources |
| Breaking Changes | Yes (v2.0.0: FastAPI rebuild) | Not specified |
| Python Requirement | AVX-capable CPU (pip path) | Python 3.11+ |
| Maintainer Type | Community (LearningCircuit) | Company-backed |

## SearXNG Support

### Local Deep Research

SearXNG is a first-class, default search backend for Local Deep Research. The project's recommended Docker deployment bundles Ollama, SearXNG, and the application itself in a single `docker-compose.yml` file, making SearXNG the out-of-the-box search layer ([dev.to](https://dev.to/arshtechpro/local-deep-research-run-your-own-ai-research-assistant-fully-private-6eg); [vdf.ai](https://vdf.ai/blog/local-deep-research/)). The project's GitHub description explicitly lists SearXNG among its supported search engines alongside arXiv, PubMed, Wikipedia, GitHub, and others ([Local Deep Research GitHub](https://github.com/LearningCircuit/local-deep-research)).

A notable security consideration was introduced in v1.10.3: SearXNG addresses on localhost or private networks are blocked by default unless the server operator explicitly approves them, because any signed-in user could otherwise point the setting at an internal service ([vdf.ai](https://vdf.ai/blog/local-deep-research/)). The Docker commands approve this by pinning the URL in the environment variable `LDR_SEARCH_ENGINE_WEB_SEARXNG_DEFAULT_PARAMS_INSTANCE_URL` ([vdf.ai](https://vdf.ai/blog/local-deep-research/)). This design choice reflects a security-first posture appropriate for a tool that stores encrypted data and handles sensitive research queries.

Local Deep Research also supports SearXNG in combination with academic search engines (arXiv, PubMed, Semantic Scholar) and general web sources (Wikipedia, GitHub, The Guardian, Wayback Machine), allowing hybrid research passes that combine multiple retrieval strategies ([dev.to](https://dev.to/arshtechpro/local-deep-research-run-your-own-ai-research-assistant-fully-private-6eg); [Local Deep Research GitHub](https://github.com/LearningCircuit/local-deep-research)).

### GPT Researcher

GPT Researcher supports SearXNG as one of over 20 retriever integrations, but it is not the default. The project defaults to Tavily, a paid, agent-optimized search API ([vdf.ai](https://vdf.ai/blog/local-deep-research/); [opensourcealternatives.to](https://www.opensourcealternatives.to/item/gpt-researcher)). To use SearXNG, operators must explicitly configure the `RETRIEVER` environment variable to `searx` and set `SEARX_URL` to point at their SearXNG instance ([vdf.ai](https://vdf.ai/blog/local-deep-research/)). The configuration example from vdf.ai shows:

```
RETRIEVER="searx"
SEARX_URL="http://localhost:8080"
```

Retrievers can be combined with commas—for example, `RETRIEVER=searx,arxiv`—enabling parallel multi-source research ([vdf.ai](https://vdf.ai/blog/local-deep-research/)). GPT Researcher also supports DuckDuckGo as a keyless retriever, providing an alternative free search path ([listenlabs.com](https://listenlabs.com/articles/best-open-source-gpt-assistants/)).

Like Local Deep Research, GPT Researcher requires that SearXNG be configured to output JSON, as SearXNG serves only HTML by default unless `json` is added to `search.formats` in `settings.yml` ([vdf.ai](https://vdf.ai/blog/local-deep-research/)). Failure to configure this results in a "403 Client Error: Forbidden" response ([vdf.ai](https://vdf.ai/blog/local-deep-research/)).

### SearXNG Support Comparison Table

| Dimension | Local Deep Research | GPT Researcher |
|-----------|-------------------|----------------|
| SearXNG Default? | Yes (bundled in Docker) | No (Tavily is default) |
| Configuration Effort | Minimal (Docker Compose) | Requires env var changes |
| JSON Output Requirement | Yes | Yes |
| Combined Retrievers | Yes (SearXNG + academic engines) | Yes (comma-separated) |
| Security Controls | Egress scopes; localhost approval | Not specified |
| Keyless Alternatives | SearXNG, DuckDuckGo | DuckDuckGo, SearXNG |
| Academic Sources via SearXNG | arXiv, PubMed, Semantic Scholar | arXiv, PubMed (direct) |

## Synthesis and Assessment

The comparison reveals two projects with fundamentally different design philosophies. Local Deep Research treats SearXNG and local inference as the primary deployment mode, with cloud providers as optional additions. Its MIT license, security-first egress controls, and encrypted storage (SQLCipher with AES-256) position it as a privacy-focused tool ([dev.to](https://dev.to/arshtechpro/local-deep-research-run-your-own-ai-research-assistant-fully-private-6eg); [vdf.ai](https://vdf.ai/blog/local-deep-research/)). GPT Researcher, by contrast, treats SearXNG as one option among many, defaulting to paid APIs that provide higher-quality results at the cost of data leaving the user's infrastructure ([opensourcealternatives.to](https://www.opensourcealternatives.to/item/gpt-researcher); [vdf.ai](https://vdf.ai/blog/local-deep-research/)).

On licensing, both projects are permissive and commercially friendly, though GPT Researcher's Apache-2.0/MIT ambiguity should be resolved before enterprise adoption. On versioning, GPT Researcher ships more frequently and has a longer track record, while Local Deep Research's v2.0.0 represents a more significant architectural overhaul. On SearXNG support specifically, Local Deep Research provides a more integrated, secure, and zero-configuration experience, while GPT Researcher offers greater flexibility in combining SearXNG with other retrievers but requires more explicit setup.

For teams prioritizing privacy and local-first operation, Local Deep Research's default SearXNG integration and egress scopes make it the stronger choice. For teams that need maximum retriever flexibility and are comfortable with paid search APIs, GPT Researcher's broader integration surface and longer maintenance history provide advantages.
